name: Autocomplete and Typeahead
intent: Suggest completions of what a user has typed so far after every keystroke, ranked by popularity, in a time short enough to feel instant, by doing the work of finding completions ahead of time.
scenario: A shop's search box shows suggestions as people type. The log gives 40 popular queries with their counts ("iphone" 9,800, "laptop" 8,100, "headphones" 7,600, down to "icon pack" 300). When someone has typed "ip", the box should show iphone, iphone 15 and ipad within roughly 100 ms, which is the time budget for the suggestion to feel like part of typing. Someone typing "iphone 15 case" makes 14 keystrokes, and 10,000 people typing it at once would make 140,000 requests.
problem: A search box asks a question on every keystroke, and each question is a prefix, not a whole word. Finding the completions by scanning every stored query is far too slow for millions of entries, and the shortest prefixes ("i", "ip") match the most of them. Returning them in alphabetical order is cheap but shows rare queries before common ones. And sending every keystroke to the backend multiplies the load by the length of the query. The method used to look up completions decides the cost per keystroke, the memory the index needs and how fresh the popularity data can be.

howItWorks.title: Sorted list and binary search
howItWorks.text: Keep all queries in one alphabetical list. Binary search finds the first entry at or after the prefix in about log2(n) steps (5 for the 40 entries and the prefix "ip"), and all completions sit next to each other from there. That is cheap in memory (one entry per query) but the scan must read every match to find the most popular ones. For "i" or "ip" the matches are a large share of the list, so the cost of the most common keystrokes grows with the data. If you only wanted alphabetical order the scan could stop after k entries, but nobody wants that order.

howItWorks.title: A trie: one node per prefix
howItWorks.text: A trie stores each query as a path of characters, so every shared prefix is stored once and finding the node for "ip" costs two steps. Collecting the completions still means visiting every node below it: 39 steps for "ip" and 78 for "i" in the 40-query example, which has 250 nodes. Memory is one node per distinct prefix. The trie finds the prefix instantly but, like the list, does work proportional to the number of completions.

howItWorks.title: Precompute the top k at every node
howItWorks.text: The fix is to do the ranking ahead of time: store the k best completions at each node. A lookup walks the prefix and reads k entries, so the cost depends on the length of the prefix and k, not on the size of the data: 5 steps for "ip" and 4 for "i" with k = 3. The price is memory (598 stored entries for 40 queries at k = 3, against 40 for the sorted list) and freshness: when a count changes, the lists on the path above it must be rebuilt, so popularity is usually refreshed in batches from query logs, not per search.

howItWorks.title: Edge n-grams in a search index
howItWorks.text: If you already run a search engine, index each query under all of its prefixes ("i", "ip", "iph", ...) as terms, called edge n-grams. A lookup is then one term and its postings list, and the engine's own scoring can rank by popularity, filter by category or tolerate a typo. In the example, "ip" reads 11 postings and the index stores 645 entries. It is the easiest way to get suggestions with existing infrastructure, at the cost of the largest index and a coarser latency than a purpose-built structure.

howItWorks.title: Rank by popularity, and cut the keystrokes
howItWorks.text: Rank by how often each query was searched, not by the alphabet: with "ip", popularity shows iphone, iphone 15, ipad, and alphabetical order shows ipad, ipad case, ipad pro. Then reduce the number of requests. A debounce waits until the typist pauses before sending: with a 200 ms debounce the 14 keystrokes of "iphone 15 case" send 3 requests, not 14. Caching the first 1 or 2 characters serves the most repeated prefixes without touching the backend: with 2 cached characters, 12 of the 14 requests still reach it. Also cancel or ignore a response that arrives after the user has typed more.

pros: Per-keystroke cost can be made independent of the number of completions by precomputing the top k
Popularity ranking shows what people actually search for
Debounce and a cache for short prefixes cut backend load by a large factor
An edge n-gram index reuses the search cluster you already operate
cons: Precomputed lists cost much more memory than the raw query list (598 against 40 entries in the example)
Popularity data is stale between rebuilds, so a trending query appears late
Every keystroke is a request unless the client debounces, caches and cancels
Suggestions of past queries can leak private or offensive ones unless filtered
whenToUse: A search box where users see suggestions after the first one or two characters
Large sets of known strings (queries, product names, addresses) with usage counts
Latency budgets of about 100 ms per suggestion request
whenNotToUse: Free-text fields with no stable set of likely completions, where there is nothing to suggest from
Tiny lists that the client can filter in memory without a request
Spelling correction or fuzzy matching on its own, which needs edit-distance methods, not prefixes
pitfalls: Ranking alphabetically, or by recency of insertion, instead of by popularity
Scanning all matches of a one-letter prefix on every request, which is the most frequent request
Sending a request on every keystroke with no debounce, cache or cancellation of stale responses
Showing a response for an old prefix after a newer one: the box flickers or shows the wrong list
Rebuilding top-k lists on every search, instead of in batches from logs
Offering suggestions from raw logs without removing private, rare or harmful queries

roles.label: User
roles.description: Types a query one character at a time.

roles.label: Search box
roles.description: Decides when to send a request: debounces, caches and ignores stale replies.

roles.label: Prefix cache
roles.description: Answers the most common short prefixes without reaching the index.

roles.label: Suggestion index
roles.description: The structure that finds and ranks completions of a prefix: a trie with top-k lists.

roles.label: Query logs
roles.description: Where the popularity counts come from, processed in batches.

quiz.question: A suggestion service stores 50 million past queries in a sorted list and answers by binary search and a scan of all matches. The one-letter prefixes are the slowest requests. Why?
options: Binary search is slower for short prefixes because they have fewer characters to compare.
A short prefix matches a huge share of the list, and the scan must read every match to find the most popular.
Short prefixes are not stored in the list, so the search falls back to a full table scan.
The list has to be re-sorted for each one-letter prefix before it can be searched.
quiz.explanation: The binary search is just as fast, but the scan is proportional to the number of matches, and one letter matches a large part of the data. Storing the top k at each prefix removes that cost. The list is already sorted and needs no extra steps.

quiz.question: A team stores the top 5 completions at every node of a trie and finds the lookup is fast, but memory use has grown several times over. What explains it?
options: The trie now stores each query's characters twice, once forward and once reversed.
Debounce and caching each keep their own copy of the whole trie.
Every node, including the many for long prefixes, holds up to 5 entries, so the index stores many entries per query.
Popularity counts are stored as text, which takes more space than numbers.
quiz.explanation: Each query appears in the list of every node on its path, up to k per node, so the stored entries are several times the number of queries (598 against 40 in the example). That is the price of a lookup that only reads k entries. Nothing is stored in reverse, and caches are separate.

quiz.question: A client currently sends a request on every keystroke. Which change cuts the backend load the most without changing what users finally see?
options: Wait for a short pause in typing before sending, and serve the first 1 or 2 characters from a cache.
Return alphabetical results, which are cheaper for the index to produce.
Send each keystroke twice and use whichever answer comes back first.
Increase k, so each response contains more suggestions.
quiz.explanation: Debounce reduces the number of requests (14 keystrokes to 3 at a 200 ms pause) and a cache removes the most repeated short prefixes. Alphabetical order makes the suggestions worse, duplicating requests increases load, and a larger k makes each response bigger.
